title: MultiFactor

Optional additional columns considered metadata. Let’s use example data set take closer look LinkMap. trade_posts() function generates data fictional trade posts, one type good traded another. particular case, types books traded types furniture. two types goods captured two columns, column names representing types good rows representing specific type-pairs traded trade post, , generally, linked LinkMap. what: Example of adjacency list formatted data
title: MultiFactor
text: ’ll format LinkMap fruit furniture generated . stored file adjacency list format, may look like :
code: # Use igraph to deconstruct a graph into an adjacency list, coerce to characters adj <- lapply( as_adj_list( as.igraph(fruit2clothing) ), as_ids ) # Only keep the 'fruit' nodes that have more than one link for now adj <- adj[ levels(fruit2clothing)$fruit ] adj <- adj[ lengths(adj) > 0 ] # collapse names to first elements of character vectors adj <- mapply(c, names(adj), adj, USE.NAMES = FALSE) adj <- vapply(adj, paste, collapse = "\t", "") pear\tdesk cherry\tchair\ttable\tdesk melon\tchair\ttable\tdesk  blueberry\tchair\tdesk # Create some temporary file to read from: temp <- tempfile() # fill the temp file with the adjacency list we just constructed  t.con <- file(temp, "w") cat(adj, file = t.con, sep = "\n") close(t.con)  adj_data <- read_adjacency_list(temp) adj_data #>       id.x    id.y #> 1   apples   dress #> 2   apples  gloves #> 3   apples     hat #> 4   apples   scarf #> 5   apples t-shirt #> 6   grapes   dress #> 7   grapes     hat #> 8   grapes   scarf #> 9   melons   dress #> 10  melons     hat #> 11  melons   scarf #> 12 oranges   dress #> 13 oranges     hat #> 14 oranges   scarf #> 15   pears  gloves #> 16   pears     hat #> 17   pears   scarf #> 18   pears t-shirt  # Notice that the unlinked data types are no longer in the graph.   plot(as.igraph(adj_data))
